1→# Phase 18: Performance Instrumentation - Context
     2→
     3→**Gathered:** 2026-03-07
     4→**Status:** Ready for planning
     5→
     6→<domain>
     7→## Phase Boundary
     8→
     9→Add IPFS/IPNS duration histograms, Kubo node health metrics scraping, and TEE batch timing to the existing Prometheus instrumentation. Capture "before" baselines via a synthetic test script on staging. This phase instruments only — no architectural changes, no client-side timing (Phase 22), no alerting.
    10→
    11→</domain>
    12→
    13→<decisions>
    14→## Implementation Decisions
    15→
    16→### Histogram bucket design
    17→
    18→- Two-tier bucket strategy: "fast" tier for DB-path operations, "slow" tier for network operations
    19→- Fast tier: exponential spacing, ~1ms to 500ms (DB resolve, local lookups)
    20→- Slow tier: exponential spacing, ~50ms to 30s upper bound (DHT resolve, IPFS pin, IPFS cat)
    21→- Extended tier for TEE republish batches: 1s to 120s (batches process multiple entries)
    22→- Exponential bucket spacing for all tiers (not linear) — better resolution where observations cluster
    23→
    24→### Kubo metrics scope
    25→
    26→- Scrape full Kubo Prometheus endpoint but only build dashboard panels for: peer count, bandwidth in/out, datastore size
    27→- Other Kubo metrics exist in Prometheus for ad-hoc queries but don't need dedicated panels
    28→- Alloy scrapes Kubo directly as a second prometheus.scrape target (ipfs:5001/debug/metrics/prometheus) — not proxied through CipherBox API
    29→- Metrics infrastructure is staging-only; local dev does not run Alloy/Prometheus
    30→
    31→### Dashboard and baseline format
    32→
    33→- Extend existing cipherbox-staging.json dashboard with new rows (not a separate dashboard)
    34→- Add IPFS/IPNS duration panels alongside existing counter panels in their respective rows
    35→- Add a new "Kubo Health" row for peer count, bandwidth, datastore panels
    36→- No Grafana alerting rules in this phase — observation only, alerts premature before baselines established
    37→- "Before" baselines documented as a markdown file in .planning/ with observed p50/p95/p99 values
    38→- Baselines captured from staging using a synthetic test script (uploads, downloads, resolves, publishes) — reproducible and comparable with Phase 22
    39→
    40→### Metric label granularity
    41→
    42→- IPFS/IPNS duration histograms carry labels: `operation` (resolve/publish/pin/cat) + `result` (success/error/timeout) + `source` (db/network, for resolve only)
    43→- TEE republish batch histogram carries `tee_provider` label (currently `mock`, later `phala`, then `nitro` in M4) — zero cardinality cost now, future-proofs comparison
    44→- Whether to add `record_type` (folder/file) to IPNS histograms: Claude's discretion based on whether code paths actually differ
    45→
    46→### Claude's Discretion
    47→
    48→- Whether IPFS pin/cat histograms carry a `size_bucket` label — depends on whether file size is easily accessible at the instrumentation point
    49→- Whether IPNS histograms carry `record_type` (folder/file) label — depends on code path divergence
    50→- Exact exponential bucket values for each tier
    51→- Synthetic test script implementation details (language, number of iterations, warm-up)
    52→- Grafana panel layout within existing rows
    53→
    54→</decisions>
    55→
    56→<code_context>
    57→
    58→## Existing Code Insights
    59→
    60→### Reusable Assets
    61→
    62→- `MetricsService` (`apps/api/src/metrics/metrics.service.ts`): Central prom-client registry with 5 gauges, 8 counters, 1 HTTP histogram. New histograms should be added here following the same pattern.
    63→- `HttpMetricsInterceptor` (`apps/api/src/metrics/http-metrics.interceptor.ts`): Already captures per-route HTTP latency with method/route/status_code labels. Covers PERF-02 requirement partially.
    64→- `MetricsModule` (`apps/api/src/metrics/metrics.module.ts`): Global module — any service can inject MetricsService.
    65→- `MetricsController` (`apps/api/src/metrics/metrics.controller.ts`): Exposes `/metrics` endpoint, excluded from Swagger.
    66→
    67→### Established Patterns
    68→
    69→- Counters incremented in controllers: `ipns.controller.ts` increments ipnsPublishes/ipnsResolves, `ipfs.controller.ts` increments fileUploads/fileDownloads
    70→- Duration timing should wrap the same call sites — add `process.hrtime.bigint()` around the IPNS service calls and IPFS provider calls
    71→- Alloy config (`docker/alloy-config.river`): scrapes API /metrics every 30s, ships to Grafana Cloud Mimir
    72→- Grafana dashboard JSON (`docker/grafana/dashboards/cipherbox-staging.json`): manually maintained, imported to Grafana Cloud
    73→
    74→### Integration Points
    75→
    76→- `apps/api/src/ipns/ipns.service.ts`: IPNS resolve and publish logic — instrument here for resolve/publish duration
    77→- `apps/api/src/ipfs/providers/local.provider.ts`: IPFS pin and cat operations — instrument here for pin/cat duration
    78→- `apps/api/src/republish/republish.processor.ts`: TEE batch processing — already has counter increments, add duration histogram
    79→- `docker/alloy-config.river`: Add second scrape target for Kubo metrics
    80→- `docker/docker-compose.staging.yml`: May need Kubo API port exposed to Alloy network
    81→
    82→</code_context>

1→# Requirements: CipherBox v1.1 IPFS Infrastructure
     2→
     3→**Defined:** 2026-03-07
     4→**Core Value:** Zero-knowledge privacy -- files encrypted client-side, server never sees plaintext
     5→
     6→## v1.1 Requirements
     7→
     8→Requirements for IPFS infrastructure milestone. Each maps to roadmap phases.
     9→
    10→### IPNS Reliability
    11→
    12→- [ ] **IPNS-01**: Self-hosted Someguy deployed alongside Kubo, replacing delegated-ipfs.dev as primary IPNS routing provider
    13→- [ ] **IPNS-02**: IPNS resolution uses DB-first strategy with async Kubo DHT verification via self-hosted Someguy
    14→- [ ] **IPNS-03**: Recovery tool resolves IPNS via self-hosted Someguy instead of delegated-ipfs.dev
    15→- [ ] **IPNS-04**: System degrades gracefully when DHT resolution is slow (timeout + DB fallback within 2s)
    16→
    17→### Vault Migration
    18→
    19→- [ ] **VAULT-01**: rootFolderKey embedded in IPFS vault blob v2 format (ECIES-wrapped in blob header)
    20→- [ ] **VAULT-02**: Client reads rootFolderKey from IPFS blob on login, falls back to DB vaults table
    21→- [ ] **VAULT-03**: Lazy migration writes vault blob v2 on next folder metadata publish
    22→- [ ] **VAULT-04**: encryptedRootIpnsPrivateKey column deprecated from vaults table (HKDF-derivable)
    23→- [ ] **VAULT-05**: Recovery tool updated to parse vault blob v2 format
    24→- [ ] **VAULT-06**: Desktop app (Rust) parses vault blob v2 format
    25→
    26→### BYO-IPFS
    27→
    28→- [ ] **BYO-01**: RemotePinningProvider implements standard IPFS Pinning Service API (pin/unpin/status)
    29→- [ ] **BYO-02**: DualPinProvider pins to both CipherBox node and user's configured node
    30→- [ ] **BYO-03**: Per-user IPFS config stored server-side (endpoint URL, encrypted auth token, provider type)
    31→- [ ] **BYO-04**: Settings UI for configuring custom IPFS node endpoint and credentials
    32→- [ ] **BYO-05**: Connection test endpoint validates user's IPFS node is reachable and API-compatible
    33→- [ ] **BYO-06**: All IPNS publishes still route through CipherBox API regardless of BYO config
    34→- [ ] **BYO-07**: Quota tracking becomes advisory for BYO users with clear UI indication
    35→
    36→### Performance Baselines
    37→
    38→- [ ] **PERF-01**: IPFS/IPNS duration histograms added to Prometheus (publish, resolve, pin, cat)
    39→- [ ] **PERF-02**: API endpoint p50/p95/p99 baselines defined per critical route
    40→- [ ] **PERF-03**: Kubo Prometheus endpoint scraped for node health metrics (peers, bandwidth, datastore)
    41→- [ ] **PERF-04**: TEE republish batch duration histogram added
    42→- [ ] **PERF-05**: Client-side timing instrumentation for encrypt/decrypt, upload/download, IPNS operations
    43→- [ ] **PERF-06**: End-to-end user journey timing captured (login-to-vault, upload-to-visible, share-to-accessible)
    44→- [ ] **PERF-07**: k6 load testing scripts simulating concurrent users (upload, download, publish, resolve)
    45→- [ ] **PERF-08**: Capacity thresholds documented with scaling recommendations
    46→
    47→## v1.2 Requirements
    48→
    49→Deferred to future release. Tracked but not in current roadmap.
    50→
    51→### IPNS Enhancements
    52→
    53→- **IPNS-05**: CRDT-based share discovery via IPNS inbox (replace server-side shares table)
    54→- **IPNS-06**: folder_ipns CID cache made advisory (IPNS becomes primary source)
    55→
    56→### Database Minimization
    57→
    58→- **DB-01**: Device registry approval workflow migrated off database
    59→- **DB-02**: pinned_cids table eliminated (alternative quota tracking via IPFS MFS or client-reported)
    60→
    61→### BYO-IPFS Advanced
    62→
    63→- **BYO-08**: Client-direct IPFS upload mode (bypass server relay for power users)
    64→
    65→## Out of Scope
    66→
    67→Explicitly excluded. Documented to prevent scope creep.
    68→
    69→| Feature                             | Reason                                                                                                                                |
    70→| ----------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
    71→| Full database elimination (zero DB) | Auth tables (users, auth_methods, refresh_tokens) require indexed queryable storage. IPFS is not a database.                          |
    72→| IPNS PubSub as primary resolution   | Only works when publisher and resolver share PubSub peers. Not persistent. Doesn't scale to thousands of IPNS names per user.         |
    73→| CRDT for all metadata               | Premature -- optimistic concurrency already solves folder conflicts. CRDTs add state size growth and cross-platform merge complexity. |
    74→| DNSLink as IPNS alternative         | Requires DNS infrastructure per user. Propagation is slow. Doesn't support per-folder/per-file IPNS model.                            |
    75→| Share migration to IPFS             | Requires CRDT inbox protocol (research-only this milestone). Complex query patterns (filter by recipient, status, revocation).        |
    76→| Encrypted Productivity Suite        | Deferred to Milestone 4 (v2.0) -- billing, teams, doc editors, signing, AWS Nitro TEE                                                 |
    77→| Mobile apps                         | Deferred to Milestone 4+                                                                                                              |

    10→} from '@nestjs/common';
    11→import { ApiTags, ApiOperation, ApiResponse, ApiBearerAuth, ApiQuery } from '@nestjs/swagger';
    12→import { Throttle, ThrottlerGuard } from '@nestjs/throttler';
    13→import { JwtAuthGuard } from '../auth/guards/jwt-auth.guard';
    14→import { IpnsService } from './ipns.service';
    15→import {
    16→  PublishIpnsDto,
    17→  PublishIpnsResponseDto,
    18→  BatchPublishIpnsDto,
    19→  BatchPublishIpnsResponseDto,
    20→  ResolveIpnsQueryDto,
    21→  ResolveIpnsResponseDto,
    22→} from './dto';
    23→import { MetricsService } from '../metrics/metrics.service';
    24→import { RequestWithUser } from '../common/types';
    25→
    26→@ApiTags('IPNS')
    27→@ApiBearerAuth()
    28→@UseGuards(JwtAuthGuard, ThrottlerGuard)
    29→@Controller('ipns')
    30→export class IpnsController {
    31→  constructor(
    32→    private readonly ipnsService: IpnsService,
    33→    private readonly metricsService: MetricsService
    34→  ) {}
    35→
    36→  // [SECURITY: HIGH-04] Rate limit IPNS publish to prevent abuse
    37→  // Each publish makes external HTTP calls to delegated-ipfs.dev
    38→  @Throttle({ default: { limit: 10, ttl: 60000 } }) // 10 publishes per minute per user
    39→  @Post('publish')
    40→  @ApiOperation({
    41→    summary: 'Publish IPNS record',
    42→    description:
    43→      'Relay a pre-signed IPNS record to the IPFS network via delegated routing. ' +
    44→      'The client signs the record locally; backend relays to delegated-ipfs.dev and tracks ' +
    45→      'the folder for TEE republishing.',
    46→  })
    47→  @ApiResponse({
    48→    status: 200,
    49→    description: 'IPNS record published successfully',
    50→    type: PublishIpnsResponseDto,
    51→  })
    52→  @ApiResponse({
    53→    status: 400,
    54→    description: 'Bad Request - Invalid record format or missing required fields',
    55→  })
    56→  @ApiResponse({
    57→    status: 401,
    58→    description: 'Unauthorized - JWT token required',
    59→  })
    60→  @ApiResponse({
    61→    status: 409,
    62→    description:
    63→      'Conflict - expectedSequenceNumber does not match current server sequence number. ' +
    64→      'Response body includes currentSequenceNumber for client re-sync.',
    65→  })
    66→  @ApiResponse({
    67→    status: 502,
    68→    description: 'Bad Gateway - Failed to publish to delegated routing',
    69→  })
    70→  async publishRecord(
    71→    @Request() req: RequestWithUser,
    72→    @Body() dto: PublishIpnsDto
    73→  ): Promise<PublishIpnsResponseDto> {
    74→    const result = await this.ipnsService.publishRecord(req.user.id, dto);
    75→    this.metricsService.ipnsPublishes.inc({ type: 'single' });
    76→    return result;
    77→  }
    78→
    79→  // [SECURITY: HIGH-04] Rate limit batch publish - lower limit since each batch can have up to 200 records
    80→  @Throttle({ default: { limit: 5, ttl: 60000 } }) // 5 batch publishes per minute per user
    81→  @Post('publish-batch')
    82→  @ApiOperation({
    83→    summary: 'Batch publish IPNS records',
    84→    description:
    85→      'Publish multiple IPNS records (folder and/or file) in a single API call. ' +
    86→      'Supports up to 200 records per batch with concurrency-limited processing. ' +
    87→      'Partial success is allowed: individual record failures do not fail the batch.',
    88→  })
    89→  @ApiResponse({
    90→    status: 200,
    91→    description: 'Batch publish results with per-record outcomes',
    92→    type: BatchPublishIpnsResponseDto,
    93→  })
    94→  @ApiResponse({
    95→    status: 400,
    96→    description: 'Bad Request - Invalid record format or batch exceeds 200 entries',
    97→  })
    98→  @ApiResponse({
    99→    status: 401,
   100→    description: 'Unauthorized - JWT token required',
   101→  })
   102→  @ApiResponse({
   103→    status: 409,
   104→    description:
   105→      'Conflict - a folder record in the batch has an expectedSequenceNumber that does not match ' +
   106→      'the current server sequence number. The entire batch is rejected.',
   107→  })
   108→  @ApiResponse({
   109→    status: 502,
   110→    description: 'Bad Gateway - Delegated routing failures (partial results may be returned)',
   111→  })
   112→  async publishBatch(
   113→    @Request() req: RequestWithUser,
   114→    @Body() dto: BatchPublishIpnsDto
   115→  ): Promise<BatchPublishIpnsResponseDto> {
   116→    const result = await this.ipnsService.publishBatch(req.user.id, dto);
   117→    this.metricsService.ipnsPublishes.inc({ type: 'batch' }, result.totalSucceeded);
   118→    return result;
   119→  }
   120→
   121→  // [SECURITY: HIGH-04] Rate limit IPNS resolve - higher limit than publish since read-only
   122→  @Throttle({ default: { limit: 30, ttl: 60000 } }) // 30 resolves per minute per user
   123→  @Get('resolve')
   124→  @ApiOperation({
   125→    summary: 'Resolve IPNS name',
   126→    description:
   127→      'Resolve an IPNS name to its current CID via delegated routing. ' +
   128→      'Returns the CID and sequence number of the current IPNS record.',
   129→  })
   130→  @ApiQuery({
   131→    name: 'ipnsName',
   132→    description:
   133→      'IPNS name to resolve. Supports CIDv1 IPNS names starting with "k51..." (PeerID-style) or "bafzaa..." (IPNS key CID).',
   134→    example: 'REDACTED',
   135→  })
   136→  @ApiResponse({
   137→    status: 200,
   138→    description: 'IPNS name resolved successfully',
   139→    type: ResolveIpnsResponseDto,
   140→  })
   141→  @ApiResponse({
   142→    status: 400,
   143→    description: 'Bad Request - Invalid IPNS name format',
   144→  })
   145→  @ApiResponse({
   146→    status: 401,
   147→    description: 'Unauthorized - JWT token required',
   148→  })
   149→  @ApiResponse({
   150→    status: 404,
   151→    description: 'Not Found - IPNS name not published or not found in routing network',
   152→  })
   153→  @ApiResponse({
   154→    status: 502,
   155→    description: 'Bad Gateway - Failed to resolve from delegated routing',
   156→  })
   157→  async resolveRecord(@Query() query: ResolveIpnsQueryDto): Promise<ResolveIpnsResponseDto> {
   158→    const result = await this.ipnsService.resolveRecord(query.ipnsName);
   159→
   160→    if (!result) {
   161→      throw new NotFoundException('IPNS name not found in routing network');
   162→    }
   163→
   164→    // Track resolve source: if signatureV2 is present, it came from the network
   165→    const source = result.signatureV2 ? 'network' : 'db_cache';
   166→    this.metricsService.ipnsResolves.inc({ source });
   167→
   168→    // Include signature fields as all-or-nothing bundle for client verification
   169→    const hasSigData = result.signatureV2 && result.data && result.pubKey;
   170→    return {
   171→      success: true,
   172→      cid: result.cid,
   173→      sequenceNumber: result.sequenceNumber,
   174→      ...(hasSigData && {
   175→        signatureV2: result.signatureV2,
   176→        data: result.data,
   177→        pubKey: result.pubKey,
   178→      }),
   179→    };
   180→  }
   181→}

## Histogram Creation with Labels

The Histogram class in TypeScript supports generic type parameters for strongly-typed labels, with the `observe()` method accepting `LabelValues<T>` and a numeric value.

## Basic Usage Example

Here's a TypeScript example of creating a histogram with labels and observing values:

```typescript
import { Histogram, Registry } from 'promclient';
const register = new Registry();
const responseTimeHistogram = new Histogram({
  name: 'http_response_time_seconds',
  help: 'HTTP response time in seconds',
  labelNames: ['endpoint'],
  buckets: [0.1, 0.5, 1, 5],
  registers: [register],
});
// Observe a response time
responseTimeHistogram.labels('/api/products').observe(0.2);
```

## Type Safety with TypeScript

TypeScript can enforce label names using `as const` - when creating a Counter (or similarly for other metrics), you can add `as const` to the labelNames to get type checking that ensures you're using valid label names.

## Working with Exemplars

When exemplars are enabled, the format for `observe()` calls changes - they get a single object with the format `{labels, value, exemplarLabels}`.

The prom-client library provides full TypeScript support with proper type definitions for histogram label handling, making it safe and straightforward to use with metrics in 2025.

Additional datastore metrics (with `*_datastore_*` naming) can be exposed on `/debug/metrics/prometheus` when using measurement-enabled profiles like flatfs-measure, badgerds-measure, or pebbleds-measure.

The `/debug/metrics/prometheus` endpoint can return metrics including http_server_* metrics, which now use a server_domain label to group requests by gateway domain.

## Recent Metrics Changes

In Kubo v0.39, the Amino DHT Sweep provider metric was renamed from `total_provide_count_total` to `provider_provides_total` to follow OpenTelemetry naming conventions.

## Peer and Connection Metrics

An optional plugin can periodically go through the node's peer store, open connections, and open streams to collect peer metrics, which are then pushed to Prometheus at a configurable interval.

Based on the search results, here's what I found about configuring Grafana Alloy's `prometheus.scrape` component with multiple targets using River configuration syntax:

## Basic Multiple Targets Example

The targets field can be populated with multiple scrape targets, such as a constant target like localhost:9001 and an expression that ties the target to another value. Here's an example:

```
prometheus.scrape "default" {
  targets = [
    { "__address__" = local.file.targets.content },
    { "__address__" = "localhost:9001" },
  ]
  forward_to = [prometheus.remote_write.default.receiver]
  scrape_config {
    job_name = "default"
  }
}
```

## Multiple Targets with Discovery

For more complex scenarios with multiple targets, the set of targets can either be static, or dynamically provided periodically by a service discovery component such as discovery.kubernetes.

A practical example from the community forums shows using discovery.dns with prometheus.scrape where targets = discovery.dns.application-foo.targets is configured to forward_to = [prometheus.remote_write...].

## Key Configuration Elements

The special label `__address__` must always be present and corresponds to the `<host>:<port>` used for the scrape request. By default, the scrape job tries to scrape all available targets' `/metrics` endpoints using HTTP, with a scrape interval of 1 minute and scrape timeout of 10 seconds. The metrics path, protocol scheme, scrape interval and timeout, query parameters, and other settings can be configured using the component's arguments.

The Grafana Alloy documentation and examples provide these patterns for configuring multiple Prometheus scrape targets in your River configuration.

## Datastore Metrics

Datastore metrics are no longer enabled by default when initializing a Kubo repository, with metrics prefixed with `<dsname>_datastore` (e.g., flatfs_datastore_..., leveldb_datastore_...) not exposed unless explicitly enabled. Convenience opt-in profiles can be enabled at initialization time with `ipfs init --profile`, including flatfs-measure, pebbleds-measure, and badgerds-measure.

## Prometheus Metrics Updates

I've completed the web search for your query. Here's a summary of what I found about Kubo IPFS metrics, bandwidth monitoring, and Prometheus integration:

## Key Findings:

**Bandwidth Monitoring:**
The `ipfs stats bw` command prints bandwidth information for the IPFS daemon, displaying TotalIn, TotalOut, RateIn, and RateOut. The command supports options to specify a peer or protocol to print bandwidth for.

**Prometheus Metrics:**
Additional datastore metrics can be exposed on /debug/metrics/prometheus when using the pebbleds-measure profile. In recent versions, the metric `total_provide_count_total` has been renamed to `provider_provides_total` to follow standard conventions.

**Swarm Peers API:**
The `ipfs swarm peers` command is only supported when the daemon is online. The RPC API endpoint for swarm peers is available at `/api/v0/swarm/peers`.

**Feature Request History:**
There has been interest in exposing bandwidth in/out metrics as given by `ipfs stats bw`, potentially split for various subsystems like DHT and Bitswap, along with repository size, object count, and peers latency distribution.

The search results show that Kubo supports bandwidth monitoring through CLI commands and has Prometheus metrics endpoints, though additional subsystem-level metrics have been historically requested but may not be fully exposed in the standard metrics endpoint.

# Prometheus Metrics Request Analysis

## Requested Metrics

The issue requests several metrics not originally exposed by IPFS:

- **Bandwidth**: "bandwidth in/out (as given by `ipfs stats bw`), potentially split for the various subsystem (DHT, bitswap ...)"
- **Repository data**: "repository size and object count (as given by `ipfs repo stat`)"
- **Peer latency**: "peers latency distribution (processed from `ipfs swarm peers --latency`)"
- **DHT metrics**: "DHT metrics (latency, failure rate ...)"

## Later User Requests

A subsequent commenter sought additional metrics including:

- IPFS status information (gateway, peer ID, public key)
- Connected peer IDs
- File and repository counts and sizes
- Pinned file listings and counts
- Block counts

## Available Metrics

The maintainer indicated that "All currently available metrics can be seen at `http://localhost:5001/debug/metrics/prometheus`" and suggested users "scraping the API yourself (possibly writing a custom prometheus exporter)" for complex data like peer listings, as including such information would "make the metrics API unusable (and really slow)."

The discussion shows an `ipfs_info` metric was later implemented to expose version information with appropriate labels.

   125→### Pattern 1: Histogram Registration in MetricsService
   126→
   127→**What:** Add new `client.Histogram` instances following the existing pattern.
   128→**When to use:** All new duration metrics.
   129→**Example:**
   130→
   131→```typescript
   132→// In MetricsService constructor, after existing httpRequestDuration
   133→this.ipfsIpnsDuration = new client.Histogram({
   134→  name: 'cipherbox_ipfs_ipns_duration_seconds',
   135→  help: 'Duration of IPFS/IPNS operations in seconds',
   136→  labelNames: ['operation', 'result', 'source'] as const,
   137→  buckets: [0.05, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2.5, 5, 10, 20, 30],
   138→  registers: [this.registry],
   139→});
   140→```
   141→
   142→### Pattern 2: Timing Wrapper Using process.hrtime.bigint()
   143→
   144→**What:** Wrap async calls with timing, matching existing HttpMetricsInterceptor pattern.
   145→**When to use:** Around each IPFS/IPNS service call.
   146→**Example:**
   147→
   148→```typescript
   149→// In IpnsService.resolveRecord()
   150→async resolveRecord(ipnsName: string) {
   151→  const startTime = process.hrtime.bigint();
   152→  let result: 'success' | 'error' | 'timeout' = 'success';
   153→  let source = 'network';
   154→  try {
   155→    // ... existing logic ...
   156→  } catch (error) {
   157→    result = 'error';
   158→    throw error;
   159→  } finally {
   160→    const durationNs = Number(process.hrtime.bigint() - startTime);
   161→    const durationSec = durationNs / 1e9;
   162→    this.metricsService.ipfsIpnsDuration
   163→      .labels('resolve', result, source)
   164→      .observe(durationSec);
   165→  }
   166→}
   167→```
   168→
   169→### Pattern 3: prom-client startTimer() Alternative
   170→
   171→**What:** Use the built-in `startTimer()` method on Histogram for cleaner code.
   172→**When to use:** When the label values are known before timing starts.
   173→**Example:**
   174→
   175→```typescript
   176→const end = this.metricsService.ipfsIpnsDuration.startTimer({ operation: 'pin' });
   177→try {
   178→  const result = await this.pinFile(data);
   179→  end({ result: 'success', source: '' });
   180→  return result;
   181→} catch (err) {
   182→  end({ result: 'error', source: '' });
   183→  throw err;
   184→}
   185→```
   186→
   187→Note: `startTimer()` returns a function that, when called, observes the elapsed time. Label values can be provided at start and/or completion. This is the recommended pattern from prom-client.
   188→
   189→### Anti-Patterns to Avoid
   190→
   191→- **Timing at the controller layer instead of service layer:** Controllers already have HttpMetricsInterceptor for HTTP-level timing. IPFS/IPNS operation timing must be at the service/provider layer to capture the actual network call duration, not the full request lifecycle.
   192→- **Using `Date.now()` for timing:** Insufficient resolution for fast operations. Use `process.hrtime.bigint()` (nanosecond precision) or `startTimer()`.
   193→- **Creating separate histograms per operation:** One histogram with an `operation` label is more queryable (can aggregate or filter). Don't create `cipherbox_ipns_resolve_duration_seconds` and `cipherbox_ipns_publish_duration_seconds` separately.
   194→- **Timing inside retry loops:** The delegated routing client has retry logic. Timing should wrap the entire call to `DelegatedRoutingClient.publish()` or `resolve()`, including retries, since that's what the caller actually waits for.
   195→

   200→| Histogram percentile math | Custom p50/p95/p99 calculation             | Prometheus `histogram_quantile()`         | Prometheus handles this natively from histogram buckets            |
   201→| Metrics registry          | Custom metric collection and serialization | prom-client Registry                      | Already in use; handles text format, content type                  |

   203→| Synthetic load generation | Custom HTTP client with timing             | `curl` + `jq` in a shell script           | Simple, reproducible, no dependencies; or `tsx` for typed approach |

   207→## Common Pitfalls
   208→
   209→### Pitfall 1: High Cardinality Labels
   210→
   211→**What goes wrong:** Adding labels like `userId`, `ipnsName`, or `cid` to histograms creates unbounded label cardinality, causing Prometheus to OOM.
   212→**Why it happens:** Temptation to add debugging detail to metrics.
   213→**How to avoid:** Only use bounded labels: `operation` (4 values), `result` (3 values), `source` (2 values), `tee_provider` (1-3 values). Total cardinality stays under 30.
   214→**Warning signs:** Prometheus scrape duration increasing, "too many time series" errors.
   215→
   216→### Pitfall 2: Bucket Boundaries Not Covering Expected Range
   217→
   218→**What goes wrong:** If all observations fall into the +Inf bucket, the histogram becomes useless for percentile calculation.
   219→**Why it happens:** Choosing bucket boundaries without knowing the actual latency distribution.
   220→**How to avoid:** Use the two-tier strategy from CONTEXT.md. The slow tier's 30s upper bound matches the IPNS polling interval -- anything beyond is already a full cycle miss. Fast tier covers 1ms-500ms for DB lookups.
   221→**Warning signs:** All histogram observations in the +Inf or first bucket.
   222→
   223→### Pitfall 3: Alloy Network Isolation
   224→
   225→**What goes wrong:** Alloy container can't reach `ipfs:5001` because they're in different Docker networks.
   226→**Why it happens:** docker-compose.staging.yml doesn't explicitly define networks; default network should work, but Kubo's API port (5001) is bound to `127.0.0.1`.
   227→**How to avoid:** Alloy accesses Kubo via Docker's internal network (service name `ipfs`), not via host-bound ports. The `127.0.0.1:5001:5001` binding is for host access. Container-to-container uses port 5001 directly. Verify by checking that Alloy can resolve `ipfs:5001`.
   228→**Warning signs:** Alloy logs showing connection refused or timeout for Kubo scrape target.
   229→
   230→### Pitfall 4: Kubo /debug/metrics/prometheus Requires API Port
   231→
   232→**What goes wrong:** Scraping the gateway port (8080) for metrics instead of the API port (5001).
   233→**Why it happens:** Confusion between Kubo's gateway (read-only, port 8080) and API (full access, port 5001).
   234→**How to avoid:** Always use `ipfs:5001/debug/metrics/prometheus` for metrics scraping. The path `/debug/metrics/prometheus` is only available on the API port.
   235→**Warning signs:** 404 responses from metrics endpoint.
   236→
   237→### Pitfall 5: Timing the Wrong Layer for IPNS Resolve
   238→
   239→**What goes wrong:** Timing only the delegated routing call, missing the DB fallback path.
   240→**Why it happens:** `resolveRecord()` in IpnsService has two sources -- network (delegatedRouting.resolve) and DB (folderIpnsRepository.findOne). The `source` label must accurately reflect which path was taken.
   241→**How to avoid:** Instrument inside `resolveRecord()` with logic to determine the source. The existing code already has this logic (checking `signatureV2` presence for network vs DB).
   242→**Warning signs:** Metrics show only network resolves but logs show DB fallbacks happening.
   243→
   244→### Pitfall 6: Dashboard Panel Y-Axis Collisions
   245→
   246→**What goes wrong:** Existing panels shift position when new panels/rows are added, breaking the dashboard layout.
   247→**Why it happens:** Grafana uses a grid layout with `gridPos` (`x`, `y`, `w`, `h`). Inserting rows requires updating all subsequent panels' `y` coordinates.
   248→**How to avoid:** Add new duration panels within existing rows (after their respective counter panels) and append the new "Kubo Health" row at the end of existing content rows (before Logs rows). Calculate y-offsets carefully.
   249→**Warning signs:** Dashboard JSON validation errors, panels overlapping.

   394→## Discretion Decisions
   395→
   396→### `size_bucket` label on IPFS pin/cat: DO NOT ADD
   397→
   398→**Reasoning:** `LocalProvider.pinFile()` receives a `Buffer` so `data.length` is available. However, adding a `size_bucket` label (e.g., `<1KB`, `1-100KB`, `100KB-1MB`, `>1MB`) increases cardinality by 4x for only modest diagnostic value. File size correlation can be done via log analysis if needed. The overhead is not justified for a baseline phase.
   399→
   400→### `record_type` label on IPNS histograms: DO NOT ADD
   401→
   402→**Reasoning:** Examining `IpnsService.publishRecord()` and `resolveRecord()`, the code paths are identical for folder and file records. The `recordType` parameter only affects the DB field value, not the network call behavior. Adding this label would double cardinality without providing actionable information. If future phases show different performance characteristics, it can be added then.

   418→## Open Questions
   419→
   420→1. **Exact Kubo v0.34 Prometheus metric names for peer count and bandwidth**
   421→   - What we know: Kubo exposes metrics at `/debug/metrics/prometheus`. libp2p swarm metrics (`libp2p_swarm_connections_opened_total`, `_closed_total`) are available in go-libp2p since v0.26. Go runtime metrics (`go_goroutines`, `process_*`) are always present. Bandwidth and peer count are NOT natively exported as Prometheus metrics in Kubo -- they are available via RPC API (`/api/v0/swarm/peers`, `/api/v0/stats/bw`).
   422→   - What's unclear: Whether Kubo v0.34 includes the go-libp2p swarm Prometheus metrics (they were added in go-libp2p v0.26, which Kubo v0.34 may or may not bundle).
   423→   - Recommendation: Deploy the Alloy scrape target first, then inspect the actual metric output from Kubo on staging. Build dashboard panels based on observed metrics. If swarm connection metrics aren't available, use `ipfs swarm peers | wc -l` via a custom exporter or accept that peer count requires the RPC API. This can be resolved during implementation.
   424→
   425→2. **LocalProvider MetricsService injection**
   426→   - What we know: `LocalProvider` is constructed manually (not via NestJS DI). `MetricsService` is injected in `IpfsController` but not available in `LocalProvider`.
   427→   - What's unclear: Best approach to inject MetricsService into LocalProvider without refactoring the provider factory.
   428→   - Recommendation: Instrument at the controller level (IpfsController already has MetricsService) rather than modifying the provider factory. The timing difference between controller-level and provider-level is negligible (the provider is called synchronously from the controller).

The milestone establishes performance baselines before making changes, replaces the unreliable delegated-ipfs.dev dependency with self-hosted IPNS resolution, migrates rootFolderKey to an IPFS vault blob (achieving true zero-knowledge server), adds BYO-IPFS node support for data sovereignty, and completes performance baselines with client-side instrumentation and load testing after all features are stable.

    27→
    28→## Phase Details

    30→### Phase 18: Performance Instrumentation
    31→
    32→**Goal**: Operators can observe IPFS/IPNS latency and API performance in Prometheus/Grafana before any architectural changes are made
    33→**Depends on**: Nothing (first phase of milestone)
    34→**Requirements**: PERF-01, PERF-02, PERF-03, PERF-04
    35→**Success Criteria** (what must be TRUE):
    36→
    37→1. Prometheus exposes duration histograms for IPNS resolve, IPNS publish, IPFS pin, and IPFS cat operations with per-operation labels
    38→2. API endpoint response times are captured at p50/p95/p99 for all critical routes (auth, IPNS resolve/publish, file upload/download, folder CRUD)
    39→3. Kubo node health metrics (peer count, bandwidth, datastore size) are visible in Prometheus via scraped Kubo endpoint
    40→4. TEE republish batch duration histogram captures per-batch timing with success/failure labels
    41→   **Plans**: TBD

    43→### Phase 19: IPNS Resolution Improvement
    44→
    45→**Goal**: Users experience reliable, fast IPNS resolution without dependency on external delegated-ipfs.dev service
    46→**Depends on**: Phase 18 (baselines must exist to measure improvement)
    47→**Requirements**: IPNS-01, IPNS-02, IPNS-03, IPNS-04
    48→**Success Criteria** (what must be TRUE):
    49→
    50→1. Self-hosted Someguy is deployed alongside Kubo and serves as the IPNS routing provider, with delegated-ipfs.dev fully removed from the resolution path
    51→2. IPNS resolution completes within 2 seconds in the normal case (DB-first with async DHT verification) and degrades gracefully to DB-only when DHT is slow
    52→3. The standalone recovery tool resolves IPNS records via self-hosted Someguy without depending on the CipherBox API or delegated-ipfs.dev
    53→4. No user-visible errors or stale metadata when the DHT is temporarily unreachable (DB fallback serves correct data)
    54→   **Plans**: TBD
    55→
    56→### Phase 20: Vault Migration
    57→
    58→**Goal**: The server stores zero crypto material -- rootFolderKey lives in the IPFS vault blob, making the server a true zero-knowledge relay
    59→**Depends on**: Phase 19 (IPNS must be reliable before making it a login-adjacent dependency)
    60→**Requirements**: VAULT-01, VAULT-02, VAULT-03, VAULT-04, VAULT-05, VAULT-06
    61→**Success Criteria** (what must be TRUE):
    62→
    63→1. New users get vault blob v2 format on first login, with rootFolderKey ECIES-wrapped in the blob header and readable without any database round-trip
    64→2. Existing users are lazily migrated to vault blob v2 on their next folder metadata publish, with the DB copy retained as a permanent fallback
    65→3. The standalone recovery tool parses vault blob v2 and extracts rootFolderKey without needing the CipherBox API or database
    66→4. The desktop app (Rust) parses vault blob v2 and uses the embedded rootFolderKey for FUSE mount initialization

   125→### Pattern 1: Histogram Registration in MetricsService
   126→
   127→**What:** Add new `client.Histogram` instances following the existing pattern.
   128→**When to use:** All new duration metrics.
   129→**Example:**
   130→
   131→```typescript
   132→// In MetricsService constructor, after existing httpRequestDuration
   133→this.ipfsIpnsDuration = new client.Histogram({
   134→  name: 'cipherbox_ipfs_ipns_duration_seconds',
   135→  help: 'Duration of IPFS/IPNS operations in seconds',
   136→  labelNames: ['operation', 'result', 'source'] as const,
   137→  buckets: [0.05, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2.5, 5, 10, 20, 30],
   138→  registers: [this.registry],
   139→});
   140→```
   141→
   142→### Pattern 2: Timing Wrapper Using process.hrtime.bigint()
   143→
   144→**What:** Wrap async calls with timing, matching existing HttpMetricsInterceptor pattern.
   145→**When to use:** Around each IPFS/IPNS service call.
   146→**Example:**
   147→
   148→```typescript
   149→// In IpnsService.resolveRecord()
   150→async resolveRecord(ipnsName: string) {
   151→  const startTime = process.hrtime.bigint();
   152→  let result: 'success' | 'error' | 'timeout' = 'success';
   153→  let source = 'network';
   154→  try {
   155→    // ... existing logic ...
   156→  } catch (error) {
   157→    result = 'error';
   158→    throw error;
   159→  } finally {
   160→    const durationNs = Number(process.hrtime.bigint() - startTime);
   161→    const durationSec = durationNs / 1e9;
   162→    this.metricsService.ipfsIpnsDuration
   163→      .labels('resolve', result, source)
   164→      .observe(durationSec);
   165→  }
   166→}
   167→```
   168→
   169→### Pattern 3: prom-client startTimer() Alternative
   170→
   171→**What:** Use the built-in `startTimer()` method on Histogram for cleaner code.
   172→**When to use:** When the label values are known before timing starts.
   173→**Example:**
   174→
   175→```typescript
   176→const end = this.metricsService.ipfsIpnsDuration.startTimer({ operation: 'pin' });
   177→try {
   178→  const result = await this.pinFile(data);
   179→  end({ result: 'success', source: '' });
   180→  return result;
   181→} catch (err) {
   182→  end({ result: 'error', source: '' });
   183→  throw err;
   184→}
   185→```
   186→
   187→Note: `startTimer()` returns a function that, when called, observes the elapsed time. Label values can be provided at start and/or completion. This is the recommended pattern from prom-client.
   188→
   189→### Anti-Patterns to Avoid
   190→
   191→- **Timing at the controller layer instead of service layer:** Controllers already have HttpMetricsInterceptor for HTTP-level timing. IPFS/IPNS operation timing must be at the service/provider layer to capture the actual network call duration, not the full request lifecycle.
   192→- **Using `Date.now()` for timing:** Insufficient resolution for fast operations. Use `process.hrtime.bigint()` (nanosecond precision) or `startTimer()`.
   193→- **Creating separate histograms per operation:** One histogram with an `operation` label is more queryable (can aggregate or filter). Don't create `cipherbox_ipns_resolve_duration_seconds` and `cipherbox_ipns_publish_duration_seconds` separately.
   194→- **Timing inside retry loops:** The delegated routing client has retry logic. Timing should wrap the entire call to `DelegatedRoutingClient.publish()` or `resolve()`, including retries, since that's what the caller actually waits for.
   195→
   196→## Don't Hand-Roll
   197→
   198→| Problem                   | Don't Build                                | Use Instead                               | Why                                                                |
   199→| ------------------------- | ------------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------ |
   200→| Histogram percentile math | Custom p50/p95/p99 calculation             | Prometheus `histogram_quantile()`         | Prometheus handles this natively from histogram buckets            |
   201→| Metrics registry          | Custom metric collection and serialization | prom-client Registry                      | Already in use; handles text format, content type                  |
   202→| Kubo health metrics       | Custom polling via `ipfs stats bw` API     | Kubo's native `/debug/metrics/prometheus` | Built-in Prometheus endpoint; Alloy scrapes directly               |
   203→| Synthetic load generation | Custom HTTP client with timing             | `curl` + `jq` in a shell script           | Simple, reproducible, no dependencies; or `tsx` for typed approach |
   204→
   205→**Key insight:** The entire metrics pipeline (collection -> scraping -> storage -> visualization) is already built. This phase only adds new metric definitions and dashboard panels.
   206→
   207→## Common Pitfalls
   208→
   209→### Pitfall 1: High Cardinality Labels
   210→
   211→**What goes wrong:** Adding labels like `userId`, `ipnsName`, or `cid` to histograms creates unbounded label cardinality, causing Prometheus to OOM.
   212→**Why it happens:** Temptation to add debugging detail to metrics.
   213→**How to avoid:** Only use bounded labels: `operation` (4 values), `result` (3 values), `source` (2 values), `tee_provider` (1-3 values). Total cardinality stays under 30.
   214→**Warning signs:** Prometheus scrape duration increasing, "too many time series" errors.
   215→
   216→### Pitfall 2: Bucket Boundaries Not Covering Expected Range
   217→
   218→**What goes wrong:** If all observations fall into the +Inf bucket, the histogram becomes useless for percentile calculation.
   219→**Why it happens:** Choosing bucket boundaries without knowing the actual latency distribution.
   220→**How to avoid:** Use the two-tier strategy from CONTEXT.md. The slow tier's 30s upper bound matches the IPNS polling interval -- anything beyond is already a full cycle miss. Fast tier covers 1ms-500ms for DB lookups.
   221→**Warning signs:** All histogram observations in the +Inf or first bucket.
   222→
   223→### Pitfall 3: Alloy Network Isolation
   224→
   225→**What goes wrong:** Alloy container can't reach `ipfs:5001` because they're in different Docker networks.
   226→**Why it happens:** docker-compose.staging.yml doesn't explicitly define networks; default network should work, but Kubo's API port (5001) is bound to `127.0.0.1`.
   227→**How to avoid:** Alloy accesses Kubo via Docker's internal network (service name `ipfs`), not via host-bound ports. The `127.0.0.1:5001:5001` binding is for host access. Container-to-container uses port 5001 directly. Verify by checking that Alloy can resolve `ipfs:5001`.
   228→**Warning signs:** Alloy logs showing connection refused or timeout for Kubo scrape target.
   229→
   230→### Pitfall 4: Kubo /debug/metrics/prometheus Requires API Port
   231→
   232→**What goes wrong:** Scraping the gateway port (8080) for metrics instead of the API port (5001).
   233→**Why it happens:** Confusion between Kubo's gateway (read-only, port 8080) and API (full access, port 5001).
   234→**How to avoid:** Always use `ipfs:5001/debug/metrics/prometheus` for metrics scraping. The path `/debug/metrics/prometheus` is only available on the API port.
   235→**Warning signs:** 404 responses from metrics endpoint.
   236→
   237→### Pitfall 5: Timing the Wrong Layer for IPNS Resolve
   238→
   239→**What goes wrong:** Timing only the delegated routing call, missing the DB fallback path.
   240→**Why it happens:** `resolveRecord()` in IpnsService has two sources -- network (delegatedRouting.resolve) and DB (folderIpnsRepository.findOne). The `source` label must accurately reflect which path was taken.
   241→**How to avoid:** Instrument inside `resolveRecord()` with logic to determine the source. The existing code already has this logic (checking `signatureV2` presence for network vs DB).
   242→**Warning signs:** Metrics show only network resolves but logs show DB fallbacks happening.
   243→
   244→### Pitfall 6: Dashboard Panel Y-Axis Collisions
   245→
   246→**What goes wrong:** Existing panels shift position when new panels/rows are added, breaking the dashboard layout.
   247→**Why it happens:** Grafana uses a grid layout with `gridPos` (`x`, `y`, `w`, `h`). Inserting rows requires updating all subsequent panels' `y` coordinates.
   248→**How to avoid:** Add new duration panels within existing rows (after their respective counter panels) and append the new "Kubo Health" row at the end of existing content rows (before Logs rows). Calculate y-offsets carefully.
   249→**Warning signs:** Dashboard JSON validation errors, panels overlapping.

   394→## Discretion Decisions
   395→
   396→### `size_bucket` label on IPFS pin/cat: DO NOT ADD
   397→
   398→**Reasoning:** `LocalProvider.pinFile()` receives a `Buffer` so `data.length` is available. However, adding a `size_bucket` label (e.g., `<1KB`, `1-100KB`, `100KB-1MB`, `>1MB`) increases cardinality by 4x for only modest diagnostic value. File size correlation can be done via log analysis if needed. The overhead is not justified for a baseline phase.
   399→
   400→### `record_type` label on IPNS histograms: DO NOT ADD
   401→
   402→**Reasoning:** Examining `IpnsService.publishRecord()` and `resolveRecord()`, the code paths are identical for folder and file records. The `recordType` parameter only affects the DB field value, not the network call behavior. Adding this label would double cardinality without providing actionable information. If future phases show different performance characteristics, it can be added then.

   418→## Open Questions
   419→
   420→1. **Exact Kubo v0.34 Prometheus metric names for peer count and bandwidth**
   421→   - What we know: Kubo exposes metrics at `/debug/metrics/prometheus`. libp2p swarm metrics (`libp2p_swarm_connections_opened_total`, `_closed_total`) are available in go-libp2p since v0.26. Go runtime metrics (`go_goroutines`, `process_*`) are always present. Bandwidth and peer count are NOT natively exported as Prometheus metrics in Kubo -- they are available via RPC API (`/api/v0/swarm/peers`, `/api/v0/stats/bw`).
   422→   - What's unclear: Whether Kubo v0.34 includes the go-libp2p swarm Prometheus metrics (they were added in go-libp2p v0.26, which Kubo v0.34 may or may not bundle).
   423→   - Recommendation: Deploy the Alloy scrape target first, then inspect the actual metric output from Kubo on staging. Build dashboard panels based on observed metrics. If swarm connection metrics aren't available, use `ipfs swarm peers | wc -l` via a custom exporter or accept that peer count requires the RPC API. This can be resolved during implementation.
   424→
   425→2. **LocalProvider MetricsService injection**
   426→   - What we know: `LocalProvider` is constructed manually (not via NestJS DI). `MetricsService` is injected in `IpfsController` but not available in `LocalProvider`.
   427→   - What's unclear: Best approach to inject MetricsService into LocalProvider without refactoring the provider factory.
   428→   - Recommendation: Instrument at the controller level (IpfsController already has MetricsService) rather than modifying the provider factory. The timing difference between controller-level and provider-level is negligible (the provider is called synchronously from the controller).

     5→## Pattern Overview
     6→
     7→**Overall:** Zero-Knowledge Encrypted Cloud Storage (Implemented)
     8→
     9→**Key Characteristics:**
    10→
    11→- Layered E2E encryption with zero-knowledge server design
    12→- Client-side cryptographic operations with server acting as relay and storage proxy
    13→- Per-folder IPNS records enabling modular sharing capabilities
    14→- v2 FilePointer schema with per-file IPNS metadata records
    15→- Two-phase authentication (Web3Auth MPC Core Kit + CipherBox backend JWT)

    17→## Layers
    18→

    22→- Location: `apps/web/`
    23→- Contains: React 18 + TypeScript + Tailwind CSS web app

    64→## Data Flow
    65→
    66→**File Upload Flow:**
    67→
    68→1. Client generates random `fileKey` (256-bit AES) and IV (96-bit)
    69→2. Client encrypts file content with AES-256-GCM
    70→3. Client wraps `fileKey` with user's `publicKey` via ECIES
    71→4. Client sends encrypted blob to backend (POST `/ipfs/upload`, multipart/form-data field `file`)
    72→5. Backend relays to IPFS (Kubo), returns CID
    73→6. Client creates per-file FileMetadata (own IPNS record): cid, fileKeyEncrypted, fileIv, size
    74→7. Client adds FilePointer to folder metadata children: nameEncrypted, nameIv, fileMetaIpnsName
    75→8. Client encrypts folder metadata with `folderKey` (AES-256-GCM)
    76→9. Client signs IPNS record with folder's Ed25519 `ipnsPrivateKey`
    77→10. Client sends signed record to backend (POST `/ipns/publish`)
    78→11. Backend publishes to IPFS network via delegated routing
    79→
    80→**Authentication Flow:**
    81→
    82→1. User authenticates via Web3Auth MPC Core Kit (email OTP, Google OAuth, magic link, or external wallet)
    83→2. Web3Auth derives deterministic ECDSA keypair (secp256k1) via MPC threshold cryptography
    84→3. Client authenticates with CipherBox backend using Web3Auth ID token (JWT)
    85→4. Backend validates via JWKS, issues access token (15min) + refresh token (7d)
    86→5. Backend returns encrypted vault keys and TEE public keys
    87→6. Client decrypts `rootFolderKey` using `privateKey` (ECIES)
    88→7. Session active until logout or token expiry
    89→
    90→**State Management:**
    91→
    92→- `privateKey`: Client RAM only, never persisted or transmitted
    93→- `rootFolderKey`: Server stores encrypted with ECIES, client decrypts on login
    94→- Folder/file keys: Stored encrypted in IPNS metadata records
    95→- `ipnsPrivateKey`: Client encrypts with TEE public key for republishing enrollment
    96→
    97→## Key Abstractions
    98→
    99→**Vault:**
   100→
   101→- Purpose: User's encrypted file storage namespace
   102→- Location: `apps/api/src/vault/`, `apps/web/src/stores/vault.store.ts`
   103→- Pattern: One vault per user, identified by `rootIpnsName`
   104→
   105→**Folder:**
   106→
   107→- Purpose: Encrypted container with child entries (files/folders)
   108→- Location: `apps/web/src/services/folder.service.ts`, `packages/crypto/src/metadata/`
   109→- Pattern: Each folder has own IPNS keypair, `folderKey` for metadata encryption
   110→
   111→**FilePointer (v2):**
   112→
   113→- Purpose: Slim reference in folder metadata pointing to per-file IPNS record
   114→- Location: `packages/crypto/src/metadata/types.ts`
   115→- Pattern: Contains encrypted name, timestamps, `fileMetaIpnsName` (reference to FileMetadata)
   116→
   117→**FileMetadata:**
   118→
   119→- Purpose: Per-file crypto material in dedicated IPNS record
   120→- Location: `packages/crypto/src/metadata/types.ts`
   121→- Pattern: Contains CID, `fileKeyEncrypted`, `fileIv`, size, encryption mode
   122→
   123→**TEE Key Epoch:**
   124→
   125→- Purpose: Rotation-safe TEE public key management
   126→- Location: `apps/api/src/republish/`, `tee-worker/src/`
   127→- Pattern: Client encrypts IPNS keys with current epoch, TEE supports previous for 4-week grace period
   128→
   129→## Entry Points
   130→
   131→**Web Application:**
   132→
   133→- Location: `apps/web/src/main.tsx`
   134→- Dev: `pnpm --filter web dev` (<http://localhost:5173>)
   135→- Routes: `/auth`, `/vault`, file browser UI
   136→
   137→**Backend API:**
   138→
   139→- Location: `apps/api/src/main.ts`
   140→- Dev: `pnpm --filter api dev` (<http://localhost:3000>)
   141→- Endpoints: auth, vault, IPFS, IPNS, shares, device-approval, republish
   142→
   143→**Desktop Application:**
   144→
   145→- Location: `apps/desktop/src/main.ts` (Tauri frontend), `apps/desktop/src-tauri/` (Rust backend)
   146→- Dev: `pnpm --filter desktop tauri dev`
   147→- Mount point: `~/CipherBox` (macOS FUSE-T SMB)
   148→
   149→**TEE Worker:**
   150→
   151→- Location: `tee-worker/src/index.ts`
   152→- Deployed to Phala Cloud
   153→
   154→## Error Handling
   155→
   156→**Strategy:** Fail-fast with user-facing error messages
   157→
   158→**Patterns:**
   159→
   160→- Web: Toast notifications for user errors, console.error for debug (see CONCERNS.md for logging tech debt)
   161→- API: HTTP status codes with structured NestJS exception filters
   162→- Desktop FUSE: Returns errno codes (EIO, ENOENT, EPERM) to kernel
   163→- IPNS delegated routing: Exponential backoff with retry (3 attempts, 1s base, 30s cap)
   164→- Token refresh: Automatic retry with queue deduplication (`apps/web/src/lib/api/client.ts`)
   165→
   166→## Cross-Cutting Concerns
   167→
   168→**Logging:**
   169→
   170→- API: NestJS Logger (structured)
   171→- Web: Direct console.\* calls (tech debt — see CONCERNS.md)
   172→- Desktop: Rust `log` crate with `env_logger`
   173→
   174→**Authentication:**
   175→
   176→- Two-phase: Web3Auth MPC Core Kit for key derivation, CipherBox backend for API tokens
   177→- Token rotation: Refresh tokens rotated on each use
   178→- Zero-knowledge: Backend never sees private keys or plaintext
   179→
   180→**Security Invariants:**
   181→
   182→- Private key exists only in client RAM, cleared on logout
   183→- All files encrypted with unique random key + IV (no deduplication)
   184→- Server stores only encrypted keys (ECIES wrapped)
   185→- TEE keys exist in enclave memory only during signing, then zeroed
   186→

1→# Coding Conventions

     4→
     5→## Naming Patterns
     6→
     7→**Files (NestJS Backend):**
     8→- All files: lowercase with hyphens (`kebab-case.ts`)
     9→- Pattern: `PascalCaseSuffix` class → `pascal-case.suffix.ts` file
    10→- Services: `[name].service.ts` (e.g., `vault.service.ts`)
    11→- Controllers: `[name].controller.ts` (e.g., `auth.controller.ts`)
    12→- Modules: `[name].module.ts` (e.g., `ipfs.module.ts`)
    13→- DTOs: `[action]-[entity].dto.ts` (e.g., `create-vault.dto.ts`)
    14→- Guards: `[name].guard.ts` (e.g., `jwt-auth.guard.ts`)
    15→- Pipes: `[name].pipe.ts` (e.g., `validation.pipe.ts`)
    16→- Unit tests: `[name].spec.ts` beside implementation
    17→- E2E tests: `[name].e2e-spec.ts` in `test/` directory
    18→- Single entry point per module directory: `index.ts`
    19→
    20→**Folders (NestJS Backend):**
    21→- Domain folders: singular (`user/`, `vault/`, `ipfs/`)
    22→- Reusable code folders: plural (`guards/`, `pipes/`, `utils/`, `filters/`)
    23→
    24→**Files (PoC/Scripts):**
    25→- Scripts use descriptive hyphenated names: `gen-private-key.ts`
    26→
    27→**Functions:**
    28→- camelCase for all functions: `hexToBytes`, `encryptName`, `publishFolderMetadata`
    29→- Prefix helper functions with verb: `logStep`, `formatBytes`, `collectChunks`
    30→- Async functions use descriptive names indicating async nature: `fetchFolderMetadata`, `waitForIpns`
    31→
    32→**Variables:**
    33→- camelCase for local variables: `privateKey`, `folderKey`, `metadataCid`
    34→- UPPER_SNAKE_CASE for constants: `TAG_SIZE`, `IV_SIZE`
    35→- Context objects named with `ctx` suffix pattern: `HarnessContext`
    36→
    37→**Types:**
    38→- PascalCase for types and interfaces: `FolderEntry`, `FileEntry`, `FolderMetadata`
    39→- Use `type` keyword (not interfaces) for data shapes
    40→- Suffixed with purpose: `Entry` for items, `State` for stateful objects, `Config` for configuration
    41→- Prefer the use of string literals over Typescript enums 
    42→
    43→**API Fields vs Database Columns (per project rules):**
    44→- API fields: camelCase (`publicKey`, `rootFolderKey`, `ipnsName`)
    45→- Database columns: snake_case (`public_key`, `root_folder_key`)

    47→## Code Style

    67→## Import Organization

    89→## Error Handling

   121→## Logging
   122→
   123→### Backend Server Logging (NestJS)
   124→
   125→**Framework:** Winston with structured JSON logging
   126→
   127→**Transport Configuration by Environment:**
   128→
   129→| Environment | Transports | Format |
   130→|-------------|------------|--------|
   131→| Local | Console (pretty-print) | Human-readable with colors |
   132→| Development | Console + Datadog/Splunk | JSON structured |
   133→| Production | Datadog/Splunk (no console) | JSON structured |
   134→
   135→**Log Levels:**
   136→- `error` - Critical failures requiring immediate attention
   137→- `warn` - Recoverable issues, degraded functionality
   138→- `info` - Significant business events (auth, API calls, IPFS operations)
   139→- `debug` - Detailed diagnostic information (dev/local only)
   140→
   141→**Structured Log Fields:**
   142→```typescript
   143→// Required fields in all log entries
   144→{
   145→  timestamp: string;      // ISO 8601 format
   146→  level: string;          // error, warn, info, debug
   147→  message: string;        // Human-readable description
   148→  service: 'cipherbox-api';
   149→  environment: string;    // local, development, production
   150→  correlationId?: string; // Request tracking across services
   151→}
   152→
   153→// Context-specific fields
   154→{
   155→  userId?: string;        // Authenticated user (never log keys!)
   156→  operation?: string;     // e.g., 'ipfs.add', 'vault.create'
   157→  duration?: number;      // Operation duration in ms
   158→  ipfsCid?: string;       // IPFS content identifier
   159→  error?: {               // Error details (errors only)
   160→    name: string;
   161→    message: string;
   162→    stack?: string;       // Dev/local only, never in prod logs
   163→  };
   164→}
   165→```
   166→
   167→**Security Requirements:**
   168→- NEVER log `privateKey`, `folderKey`, `fileKey`, or any encryption keys
   169→- NEVER log full request/response bodies containing sensitive data
   170→- Sanitize user input before logging
   171→- Stack traces only in local/dev environments
   172→
   173→**Winston Setup Example:**
   174→```typescript
   175→import { WinstonModule } from 'nest-winston';
   176→import * as winston from 'winston';
   177→
   178→// Configure based on NODE_ENV
   179→const transports: winston.transport[] = [];
   180→
   181→if (process.env.NODE_ENV === 'local') {
   182→  transports.push(new winston.transports.Console({
   183→    format: winston.format.combine(
   184→      winston.format.colorize(),
   185→      winston.format.simple(),
   186→    ),
   187→  }));
   188→} else {
   189→  // Dev/Prod: JSON format for log aggregation
   190→  transports.push(new winston.transports.Console({
   191→    format: winston.format.json(),
   192→  }));
   193→  // Add Datadog/Splunk transport here
   194→}
   195→```
   196→
   197→### PoC/Script Logging
   198→
   199→**Framework:** Native `console` methods (PoC only)
   200→
   201→**Patterns:**
   202→- Use `console.log()` for standard output and progress
   203→- Use `console.warn()` for non-fatal issues
   204→- Use `console.error()` for fatal errors
   205→- Use helper functions for formatted output: `logStep()` for section headers

   207→**Log Format Examples:**

   212→};

   224→- Document disabled/stubbed functionality with reason
   225→- No JSDoc comments observed in codebase

   227→
   228→**Example:**

   231→    // The routing API is not available in ipfs-http-client v60.

   235→
   236→**Underscore Prefix:**
   237→- Use `_` prefix for intentionally unused parameters: `_ctx`, `_ipnsName`
   238→
   239→## Function Design
   240→
   241→**Size:**
   242→- Functions are focused and single-purpose
   243→- Typical function length: 10-30 lines
   244→- Complex operations broken into helper functions
   245→
   246→**Parameters:**
   247→- Use typed parameters with explicit types
   248→- Context objects passed as first parameter when needed (`ctx: HarnessContext`)
   249→- Optional parameters use `?` syntax or default values
   250→
   251→**Return Values:**

   254→- Async functions return `Promise<T>`

   256→## Module Design
   257→
   258→**Exports:**
   259→- POC uses single-file architecture (no exports needed)
   260→- For multi-file modules, prefer named exports

   262→**Barrel Files:**
   263→- Not used in current codebase
   264→
   265→## Binary Data Handling
   266→
   267→**Critical Convention (per project rules):**
   268→- Use `Uint8Array` for all binary data, not strings
   269→- Convert between formats using helper functions:
   270→
   271→```typescript
   272→const hexToBytes = (hex: string): Uint8Array => {
   273→    const normalized = hex.startsWith("0x") ? hex.slice(2) : hex;
   274→    return Uint8Array.from(Buffer.from(normalized, "hex"));
   275→};
   276→
   277→const bytesToHex = (bytes: Uint8Array): string => Buffer.from(bytes).toString("hex");
   278→
   279→const utf8ToBytes = (value: string): Uint8Array => Buffer.from(value, "utf8");
   280→const bytesToUtf8 = (value: Uint8Array): string => Buffer.from(value).toString("utf8");
   281→```

   283→## Cryptographic Conventions

   287→- ECIES for key wrapping
   288→- 12-byte IVs, 16-byte auth tags
   289→
   290→**Key Handling:**
   291→- Never log keys
   292→- Never store keys in localStorage/sessionStorage
   293→- Clear sensitive data after use

1→import {
     2→  Controller,
     3→  Post,
     4→  Get,
     5→  Body,
     6→  Query,
     7→  UseGuards,
     8→  Request,
     9→  NotFoundException,
    10→} from '@nestjs/common';
    11→import { ApiTags, ApiOperation, ApiResponse, ApiBearerAuth, ApiQuery } from '@nestjs/swagger';
    12→import { Throttle, ThrottlerGuard } from '@nestjs/throttler';
    13→import { JwtAuthGuard } from '../auth/guards/jwt-auth.guard';
    14→import { IpnsService } from './ipns.service';
    15→import {
    16→  PublishIpnsDto,
    17→  PublishIpnsResponseDto,
    18→  BatchPublishIpnsDto,
    19→  BatchPublishIpnsResponseDto,
    20→  ResolveIpnsQueryDto,
    21→  ResolveIpnsResponseDto,
    22→} from './dto';
    23→import { MetricsService } from '../metrics/metrics.service';
    24→import { RequestWithUser } from '../common/types';
    25→
    26→@ApiTags('IPNS')
    27→@ApiBearerAuth()
    28→@UseGuards(JwtAuthGuard, ThrottlerGuard)
    29→@Controller('ipns')
    30→export class IpnsController {
    31→  constructor(
    32→    private readonly ipnsService: IpnsService,
    33→    private readonly metricsService: MetricsService
    34→  ) {}
    35→
    36→  // [SECURITY: HIGH-04] Rate limit IPNS publish to prevent abuse
    37→  // Each publish makes external HTTP calls to delegated-ipfs.dev
    38→  @Throttle({ default: { limit: 10, ttl: 60000 } }) // 10 publishes per minute per user
    39→  @Post('publish')
    40→  @ApiOperation({
    41→    summary: 'Publish IPNS record',
    42→    description:
    43→      'Relay a pre-signed IPNS record to the IPFS network via delegated routing. ' +
    44→      'The client signs the record locally; backend relays to delegated-ipfs.dev and tracks ' +
    45→      'the folder for TEE republishing.',
    46→  })
    47→  @ApiResponse({
    48→    status: 200,
    49→    description: 'IPNS record published successfully',
    50→    type: PublishIpnsResponseDto,
    51→  })
    52→  @ApiResponse({
    53→    status: 400,
    54→    description: 'Bad Request - Invalid record format or missing required fields',
    55→  })
    56→  @ApiResponse({
    57→    status: 401,
    58→    description: 'Unauthorized - JWT token required',
    59→  })
    60→  @ApiResponse({
    61→    status: 409,
    62→    description:
    63→      'Conflict - expectedSequenceNumber does not match current server sequence number. ' +
    64→      'Response body includes currentSequenceNumber for client re-sync.',
    65→  })
    66→  @ApiResponse({
    67→    status: 502,
    68→    description: 'Bad Gateway - Failed to publish to delegated routing',
    69→  })
    70→  async publishRecord(
    71→    @Request() req: RequestWithUser,

    Usage: `./scripts/baseline-benchmark.sh <api-url> <jwt-token>`

    The script should:

    - Use `curl` with `-w "%{time_total}\n"` for client-side timing (not for Prometheus -- this is for the baselines doc)
    - Exercise these operations:

    a. **IPNS Resolve** (20 iterations): `GET /ipns/resolve?ipnsName=<ipnsName>` -- use the user's root IPNS name (must be provided or discovered via `GET /vault`).

    b. **File Upload** (20 iterations): `POST /ipfs/upload` with a small test file (generate a 10KB random blob inline with `dd if=/dev/urandom bs=10240 count=1`). Collect the CID for use in download test.

    c. **File Download** (20 iterations): `GET /ipfs/<cid>` using a CID from the upload test.

# Roadmap: CipherBox v1.1 IPFS Infrastructure

## Overview

CipherBox v1.1 transforms the platform from "IPFS as a storage backend with database fallbacks" to "IPFS-native with the database serving only auth." The milestone establishes performance baselines before making changes, replaces the unreliable delegated-ipfs.dev dependency with self-hosted IPNS resolution, migrates rootFolderKey to an IPFS vault blob (achieving true zero-knowledge server), adds BYO-IPFS node support for data sovereignty, and completes performance baselines with client-side instrumentation and load testing after all features are stable.

## Milestones

- **v0.1 Staging MVP** - Phases 1-10 (shipped 2026-02-11)
- **v1.0 Production** - Phases 11-17.1 (shipped 2026-03-05)
- **v1.1 IPFS Infrastructure** - Phases 18-22 (in progress)

## Phases

**Phase Numbering:**

- Integer phases (1, 2, 3): Planned milestone work
- Decimal phases (2.1, 2.2): Urgent insertions (marked with INSERTED)

Decimal phases appear between their surrounding integers in numeric order.

- [ ] **Phase 18: Performance Instrumentation** - Server-side Prometheus histograms and Kubo metrics scraping to establish baselines before any architectural changes
- [ ] **Phase 19: IPNS Resolution Improvement** - Replace delegated-ipfs.dev with DB-first resolution and self-hosted Someguy, achieving sub-2s resolution with >99.5% availability
- [ ] **Phase 20: Vault Migration** - Move rootFolderKey to IPFS vault blob v2 format, making the server store zero crypto material
- [ ] **Phase 21: BYO-IPFS Node Support** - User-configurable IPFS pinning endpoint with dual-pin strategy, Settings UI, and connection testing
- [ ] **Phase 22: Performance Baselines Completion** - Client-side timing instrumentation, end-to-end journey timing, k6 load testing, and capacity documentation

## Phase Details

### Phase 18: Performance Instrumentation

**Goal**: Operators can observe IPFS/IPNS latency and API performance in Prometheus/Grafana before any architectural changes are made
**Depends on**: Nothing (first phase of milestone)
**Requirements**: PERF-01, PERF-02, PERF-03, PERF-04
**Success Criteria** (what must be TRUE):

1. Prometheus exposes duration histograms for IPNS resolve, IPNS publish, IPFS pin, and IPFS cat operations with per-operation labels
2. API endpoint response times are captured at p50/p95/p99 for all critical routes (auth, IPNS resolve/publish, file upload/download, folder CRUD)
3. Kubo node health metrics (peer count, bandwidth, datastore size) are visible in Prometheus via scraped Kubo endpoint
4. TEE republish batch duration histogram captures per-batch timing with success/failure labels

**Plans:** 2 plans

Plans:
- [ ] 18-01-PLAN.md -- Add IPFS/IPNS + TEE duration histograms to MetricsService and instrument service/controller timing
- [ ] 18-02-PLAN.md -- Add Kubo scrape to Alloy, extend Grafana dashboard, create baseline benchmark script

### Phase 19: IPNS Resolution Improvement

**Goal**: Users experience reliable, fast IPNS resolution without dependency on external delegated-ipfs.dev service
**Depends on**: Phase 18 (baselines must exist to measure improvement)
**Requirements**: IPNS-01, IPNS-02, IPNS-03, IPNS-04
**Success Criteria** (what must be TRUE):

1. Self-hosted Someguy is deployed alongside Kubo and serves as the IPNS routing provider, with delegated-ipfs.dev fully removed from the resolution path
2. IPNS resolution completes within 2 seconds in the normal case (DB-first with async DHT verification) and degrades gracefully to DB-only when DHT is slow
3. The standalone recovery tool resolves IPNS records via self-hosted Someguy without depending on the CipherBox API or delegated-ipfs.dev
4. No user-visible errors or stale metadata when the DHT is temporarily unreachable (DB fallback serves correct data)
   **Plans**: TBD

### Phase 20: Vault Migration

**Goal**: The server stores zero crypto material -- rootFolderKey lives in the IPFS vault blob, making the server a true zero-knowledge relay
**Depends on**: Phase 19 (IPNS must be reliable before making it a login-adjacent dependency)
**Requirements**: VAULT-01, VAULT-02, VAULT-03, VAULT-04, VAULT-05, VAULT-06
**Success Criteria** (what must be TRUE):

1. New users get vault blob v2 format on first login, with rootFolderKey ECIES-wrapped in the blob header and readable without any database round-trip
2. Existing users are lazily migrated to vault blob v2 on their next folder metadata publish, with the DB copy retained as a permanent fallback
3. The standalone recovery tool parses vault blob v2 and extracts rootFolderKey without needing the CipherBox API or database
4. The desktop app (Rust) parses vault blob v2 and uses the embedded rootFolderKey for FUSE mount initialization
5. The encryptedRootIpnsPrivateKey column is deprecated from the vaults table (HKDF derivation is the canonical path)
   **Plans**: TBD

### Phase 21: BYO-IPFS Node Support

**Goal**: Users can configure their own IPFS node for data sovereignty, with files pinned to both CipherBox and their personal node
**Depends on**: Phase 19 (stable IPNS resolution benefits BYO workflows)
**Requirements**: BYO-01, BYO-02, BYO-03, BYO-04, BYO-05, BYO-06, BYO-07
**Success Criteria** (what must be TRUE):

1. A user can enter their IPFS node endpoint and credentials in Settings, test the connection, and see a success/failure result
2. After configuring a BYO node, every file upload is pinned to both the CipherBox node (always) and the user's node (best-effort mirror)
3. All IPNS publishes still route through the CipherBox API regardless of BYO configuration (no bypass of optimistic concurrency)
4. BYO users see an advisory quota display (not enforced) with clear indication that storage is managed by their own node
5. The connection test endpoint validates reachability and API compatibility of the user's node before saving configuration
   **Plans**: TBD

### Phase 22: Performance Baselines Completion

**Goal**: Complete performance picture exists -- client-side timing, end-to-end journeys, load test results, and capacity recommendations are documented
**Depends on**: Phase 21 (all features must be stable to produce meaningful baselines)
**Requirements**: PERF-05, PERF-06, PERF-07, PERF-08
**Success Criteria** (what must be TRUE):

1. Client-side timing instrumentation captures encrypt/decrypt throughput, upload/download duration, and IPNS operation timing in the browser
2. End-to-end user journey timings are captured for login-to-vault, upload-to-visible, and share-to-accessible workflows
3. k6 load test scripts simulate concurrent users performing upload, download, publish, and resolve operations with documented pass/fail thresholds
4. Capacity thresholds are documented with scaling recommendations (max concurrent users, storage growth projections, IPNS publish throughput limits)
   **Plans**: TBD

## Progress

**Execution Order:**
Phases execute in numeric order: 18 -> 19 -> 20 -> 21 -> 22

| Phase                              | Milestone | Plans Complete | Status      | Completed |
| ---------------------------------- | --------- | -------------- | ----------- | --------- |
| 18. Performance Instrumentation    | v1.1      | 0/2            | Planning    | -         |
| 19. IPNS Resolution Improvement    | v1.1      | 0/?            | Not started | -         |
| 20. Vault Migration                | v1.1      | 0/?            | Not started | -         |
| 21. BYO-IPFS Node Support          | v1.1      | 0/?            | Not started | -         |
| 22. Performance Baselines Complete | v1.1      | 0/?            | Not started | -         |

---

    20→- Slow tier: exponential spacing, ~50ms to 30s upper bound (DHT resolve, IPFS pin, IPFS cat)
    21→- Extended tier for TEE republish batches: 1s to 120s (batches process multiple entries)
    22→- Exponential bucket spacing for all tiers (not linear) — better resolution where observations cluster
    23→
    24→### Kubo metrics scope
    25→
    26→- Scrape full Kubo Prometheus endpoint but only build dashboard panels for: peer count, bandwidth in/out, datastore size
    27→- Other Kubo metrics exist in Prometheus for ad-hoc queries but don't need dedicated panels
    28→- Alloy scrapes Kubo directly as a second prometheus.scrape target (ipfs:5001/debug/metrics/prometheus) — not proxied through CipherBox API

   125→### Pattern 1: Histogram Registration in MetricsService
   126→
   127→**What:** Add new `client.Histogram` instances following the existing pattern.
   128→**When to use:** All new duration metrics.
   129→**Example:**
   130→
   131→```typescript
   132→// In MetricsService constructor, after existing httpRequestDuration
   133→this.ipfsIpnsDuration = new client.Histogram({
   134→  name: 'cipherbox_ipfs_ipns_duration_seconds',
   135→  help: 'Duration of IPFS/IPNS operations in seconds',
   136→  labelNames: ['operation', 'result', 'source'] as const,
   137→  buckets: [0.05, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2.5, 5, 10, 20, 30],
   138→  registers: [this.registry],
   139→});
   140→```
   141→
   142→### Pattern 2: Timing Wrapper Using process.hrtime.bigint()
   143→
   144→**What:** Wrap async calls with timing, matching existing HttpMetricsInterceptor pattern.
   145→**When to use:** Around each IPFS/IPNS service call.
   146→**Example:**
   147→
   148→```typescript
   149→// In IpnsService.resolveRecord()
   150→async resolveRecord(ipnsName: string) {
   151→  const startTime = process.hrtime.bigint();
   152→  let result: 'success' | 'error' | 'timeout' = 'success';
   153→  let source = 'network';
   154→  try {
   155→    // ... existing logic ...
   156→  } catch (error) {
   157→    result = 'error';
   158→    throw error;
   159→  } finally {
   160→    const durationNs = Number(process.hrtime.bigint() - startTime);
   161→    const durationSec = durationNs / 1e9;
   162→    this.metricsService.ipfsIpnsDuration
   163→      .labels('resolve', result, source)
   164→      .observe(durationSec);
   165→  }
   166→}
   167→```
   168→
   169→### Pattern 3: prom-client startTimer() Alternative
   170→
   171→**What:** Use the built-in `startTimer()` method on Histogram for cleaner code.
   172→**When to use:** When the label values are known before timing starts.
   173→**Example:**
   174→
   175→```typescript
   176→const end = this.metricsService.ipfsIpnsDuration.startTimer({ operation: 'pin' });
   177→try {
   178→  const result = await this.pinFile(data);
   179→  end({ result: 'success', source: '' });
   180→  return result;
   181→} catch (err) {
   182→  end({ result: 'error', source: '' });
   183→  throw err;
   184→}
   185→```
   186→
   187→Note: `startTimer()` returns a function that, when called, observes the elapsed time. Label values can be provided at start and/or completion. This is the recommended pattern from prom-client.
   188→
   189→### Anti-Patterns to Avoid
   190→
   191→- **Timing at the controller layer instead of service layer:** Controllers already have HttpMetricsInterceptor for HTTP-level timing. IPFS/IPNS operation timing must be at the service/provider layer to capture the actual network call duration, not the full request lifecycle.
   192→- **Using `Date.now()` for timing:** Insufficient resolution for fast operations. Use `process.hrtime.bigint()` (nanosecond precision) or `startTimer()`.
   193→- **Creating separate histograms per operation:** One histogram with an `operation` label is more queryable (can aggregate or filter). Don't create `cipherbox_ipns_resolve_duration_seconds` and `cipherbox_ipns_publish_duration_seconds` separately.
   194→- **Timing inside retry loops:** The delegated routing client has retry logic. Timing should wrap the entire call to `DelegatedRoutingClient.publish()` or `resolve()`, including retries, since that's what the caller actually waits for.
   195→
